summary: The Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator is a free, no-sign-up health tool. Fill in the 6 fields it asks for and it works out history of ischemic heart disease? straight away, with the formula shown underneath. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator work?
sections.html:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports history of ischemic heart disease? in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (history of cerebrovascular disease?, history of congestive heart failure? and pre-surgery creatinine level >2 Mg/d l (176.8 µmol/L)?); then you type in the total RCRI points.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

History of ischemic heart disease?=-history of cerebrovascular disease? − history of congestive heart failure? − pre-surgery creatinine level >2 mg ÷ dL (176.8 µmol ÷ L)? − pre-surgery treatment with insulin? + total RCRI points − high risk noncardiac surgery?
30-day risk of death, MI, or cardiac arrest=(total RCRI points)
Class=(total RCRI points)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take History of cerebrovascular disease? set to No, History of congestive heart failure? set to No, History of ischemic heart disease? set to No and Pre-surgery creatinine level >2 Mg/d l (176.8 µmol/L)? set to No. The calculator returns Total RCRI points = 10.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Total RCRI points = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from History of cerebrovascular disease? set to No and History of congestive heart failure? set to No.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the total RCRI points — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns history of ischemic heart disease?, derived from the total RCRI points. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total RCRI points, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Total RCRI points = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Revised Cardiac Risk Index calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
